To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the correlation between diet, as measured in terms of food consumption, and cancer mortality rates is statistically significant; (b) the correlation is stronger in males than in females; (c) the strongest correlations are found in stomach and colon cancer mortality rates; (d) the strongest positive correlations are found with fat, animal protein and saturated fatty acids; and (e) the strongest negative correlations are found with vegetable protein, fibre, carbohydrates and vitamins C and B _{1}.
the relationship between diet and cancer mortality is positive for saturated fatty acids and negative for vegetable proteins, carbohydrates, fibre and vitamins.

(a) a 1-g decrease in animal fat would lead to a decrease of two cases of cancer out of 100; (b) a 1 g increase in vegetable protein would lead to a reduction of 3.5 cases of cancer out 100; (c) a 1g increase in fibre would lead to a further reduction of 4.5 cases of cancers out of 100.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the correlation of the mortality rates for cancer with diet in Italy, and with the study of possible relationships between diet and the incidence of cancer in the Italian population.
the study of the relationship between the food consumed in different Italian areas and the cancer mortality rates in the same areas.
